The cursor blinks. A little rectangular pulse of light against a pale grey void, demanding something, anything, in return for its existence. It is the modern-day equivalent of the blank page, though somehow less romantic. Ink smells like history and mistakes; pixels just smell like warm plastic and dust. 

We live in an age of an unprecedented number of words. Between emails, texts, tweets, Slack messages, captions, and comments, humanity is churning out a linguistic Niagara Falls every single second. Most of it is garbage. “LOL,” “Sounds good,” “Will do,” “Per my last email.” We are drowning in a sea of micro-communication, yet sometimes, sitting down to write a thousand words feels like trying to move a mountain with a teaspoon.

Why do we do it? Why pull thoughts out of the messy, contradictory soup of the brain and force them into linear, orderly rows of letters? 

Maybe it’s because thinking is a messy business. Thoughts don’t arrive in sentences. They arrive in flashes—a feeling, a memory, a color, a half-formed urge. It’s like weather. But writing forces the weather into a pipe. It makes the intangible tangible. It’s a trick of alchemy: you take the invisible electricity of your consciousness and turn it into physical marks on a screen (or paper) that someone else can look at, months or centuries later, and recreate your exact state of mind in *theirs*. 

Telepathy. Reading is actual, functioning telepathy. 

Consider how miraculous that is. I am sitting here, wherever *here* is, pressing my fingers onto plastic keys. Those presses send electrical signals through circuits, across routers, perhaps up into a satellite orbiting the Earth, down into a server farm humming in a dark room, and eventually onto your screen. And just by looking at these strange little symbols—A, B, C—your brain is conjuring a voice. My voice. You are hearing the cadence of these sentences inside your own skull. We might never meet. We might live on opposite sides of a vast ocean, separated by decades of time and entirely different realities, yet right now, my mind is whispering directly into yours.

It’s quiet in this room. Just the hum of the refrigerator in the kitchen and the distant, muffled thrum of traffic outside. The kind of traffic noise that sounds like the ocean if you squint your ears just right. 

I wonder what the world looks like where you are reading this. Are you sitting on a crowded train, clutching a handrail while commuters jostle past? Are you curled up on a worn-out couch with a cat sleeping on your knees? Are you sitting at a desk under the sterile, buzzing fluorescent lights of an office you desperately want to leave? 

Context changes everything. The exact same sentence reads entirely differently depending on whether you are falling in love, grieving a loss, bored out of your mind, or half-asleep. Words are chameleons. They take on the color of whatever surface they land on. 

Right now, the surface is blank, and I am just filling it. No plan, no grand thesis statement, no outline to guide the way. Just following the thread. One sentence leads to the next, like stepping stones across a creek. You don’t need to see the other side of the water to take the next step; you just need to trust that the ground will hold your weight.

That’s a good metaphor for life, isn’t it? We spend so much time trying to engineer the entire bridge before we’ve even crossed the first plank. We want guarantees. We want a 10-step plan, a safety net, a forecast with a 100% chance of success. But the best things—the best art, the best conversations, the best mistakes—happen when you just start walking and figure it out as you go.

The sun is shifting outside the window. A beam of golden late-afternoon light just crept across the floorboards, illuminating the dust motes dancing in the air. They tumble and spin, weightless, caught in an invisible thermal current. They don’t know where they are going, either. They are just riding the current. 

There is a strange comfort in letting go of the need to be profound. We put so much pressure on ourselves to make every output *count*. Every project has to be a masterpiece; every conversation has to be meaningful; every day has to be productive. But sometimes, it’s enough just to exist. To breathe in, breathe out, and put one word after another until the timer goes off. 

A thousand words is a strange unit of measurement. It’s not very long, in the grand scheme of a novel or a life. But it’s long enough to say something true, or at least to clear out some of the mental cobwebs. It’s long enough to get lost in your own thoughts and find your way back out again.

My fingers are moving faster now, building a rhythm. *Clack-clack-clack.* It sounds like rain on a tin roof, or a typewriter in an old noir film. There is a physical satisfaction to typing. The tactile resistance of the keys, the satisfying *click* at the bottom of the stroke. In a world where everything is smooth, glass, and frictionless—touchscreens that offer no resistance, buttons that are just pixels—the mechanical keyboard is a stubborn holdout of the physical world. It reminds you that you are a body, operating levers and pulleys, interacting with reality.

We spend so much time in our heads, floating in the digital ether, that we forget we are made of meat and bone. We forget that we need sunlight and water and the smell of pine trees. We need to touch things that aren't screens. 

Maybe that’s why I write. To anchor myself. To take the chaotic, swirling storm of being a human being and pin it down to a page, just for a moment, so I can look at it and say: *Ah. There I am. That’s what I was thinking.*

The word count is ticking up. We are nearing the end of the journey, this impromptu hike through the landscape of a random brain. Soon, the cursor will stop blinking. The document will be saved. I will stand up, stretch my legs, and walk back into the kitchen to see about dinner, or make a cup of tea, leaving these words behind like footprints in the sand.

The tide will come in. The internet will scroll down. New words will wash over the old ones, burying them deep beneath the digital sediment. And that’s okay. Not everything has to last forever to matter. Some things are just for right now. 

Like a breath of air. Like a beam of afternoon light. Like a glance exchanged with a stranger on a train. 

Thank you for walking with me for a thousand words. I hope the weather is nice wherever you are.
